Archives · Cryptography · History

Europe, through its ciphered letters.

From diplomatic letters to telegrams: recover the texts, understand their stakes and show how they can be read.

This journal opens with two letters from Marie de’ Medici to her ambassador in Rome. The images, proposed readings and uncertainties can be examined together.

1713–1714

Copenhagen · Lübeck · Great Northern War

Copenhagen, 1714: Stenbock’s failed escape

A prisoner of the King of Denmark, Magnus Stenbock writes in cipher, plans an escape by sea and petitions Charles XII; the postmaster Erlund read it all. The letters to Malmberg, already deciphered by Erlund in 1714, checked; the petition, in another code, read in part (about 83%).

1759–1760

Montréal · Quebec · Seven Years’ War

Montréal, 1759–1760: “the loss of the colony”, Vaudreuil writes in cipher to the minister

Famine, three fronts, and Montcalm holding the colony lost: in spring 1759 the governor of New France tells the minister, “for you alone” and in cipher, what he cannot say in clear. Four letters never printed, read with the period table of 1757 (three read, the last in part).

1778–1779

Martinique · Dominica · American War

Martinique, 1778–1779: Bouillé and Grasse, a war plan in cipher

Bouillé has just taken Dominica, but he is 817 men short. A year later, with the comte de Grasse, he sends the minister, all in cipher, a plan to defend the islands in winter and strike as far as Newfoundland the rest of the year: the pattern of the 1781 campaign. Pieces catalogued as “not deciphered”, read with the table of Bouillé’s cipher (97.8% and 96.7%).

1648

Madrid · Rome · Spain and the Holy See

Rome, 1648: “in no case”, Philip IV wants to keep his nuncio, the future Clement IX

Innocent X renews his nuncios; Philip IV wants to keep his own, Giulio Rospigliosi, and writes in cipher to Cardinal Albornoz: “there can be no more suitable instrument” for the service of “his prince and mine”. Nineteen years later Rospigliosi becomes Clement IX. A letter never deciphered, read (98.3% of groups).

1578

Madrid · Netherlands · Philip II

Madrid, 1578: “not a real”, Antonio Pérez writes in cipher to Don John of Austria

August 1578: Don John of Austria asks for money for the army of Flanders. Antonio Pérez, who had his secretary Escobedo killed in March, answers in his own hand, cordial in clear; in cipher, the Council of Finance has “not a real” and this loan will be the last. Don John dies six weeks later. Read (98.6%), with the RAH image.

1526

Rome · French court · Italian Wars

Rome, 1526: “the Pope has fled”, what Raince put in cipher for Montmorency

Francis I’s agent in Rome writes in cipher what he cannot say in clear: in May, the quarrels at Charles V’s court; in November, after the Colonna raid, a Clement VII who sighs, speaks of fleeing Rome and blames France. Two passages never deciphered, read (97.3% and 98.0%), with the Gallica images.

1812

Madrid · Andalusia · Peninsular War

The Tagus, 1812: eight weeks before Salamanca, Jourdan’s ciphered order to Soult

May 1812: Hill has just cut the bridge at Almaraz. From Madrid, Jourdan orders Soult in cipher to reinforce d’Erlon or bring him across the Tagus to cover Madrid. Intercepted, the letter survives in a Spanish translation that leaves the numbers blank. Read with the table of the 1812 Grand Chiffre (97.0%).

1783

St Petersburg · Philadelphia · American Revolution

St Petersburg, 1783: “there is no Minister here”

For twenty months the envoy of the American Congress, Francis Dana, has waited for Catherine II to receive him. His despatch of April 1783 ends with eight lines of numbers that the 1889 edition does not print. Read with his own table, found in the same volume: in St Petersburg “there is no Minister”. Read (95.8% of groups directly).

1630

Madrid · Milan · War of the Mantuan Succession

Casale, 1630: what Philip IV wrote in cipher after Mazarin’s coup

October 1630: before Casale, the young Mazarini stops a battle between the French and the Spanish. On 6 December Philip IV answers his governor of Milan in cipher: approve the agreement, make peace before March, investigate the army in secret, and “not spend a single real amiss”. A letter left “sin descifrar”, read (97.4% of words).

1814

London · Christiania · Norwegian independence

London, 1814: a crown for Norway, a princess for its king

June 1814: Norway has given itself a constitution and a king, Christian Frederik, whom nobody recognises. In London his envoy Carsten Anker learns that Princess Charlotte of Wales has broken with the Prince of Orange, and writes in cipher: the king must not bind himself. One leaf read (98.8% of signs), missing from the printed 1814 correspondence.

1520

Valladolid · Tordesillas · Revolt of the Comuneros

Castile, 1520: what the governors wrote to Charles V in cipher

In September the regent Adrian of Utrecht writes in cipher that the Junta means to take the alcabalas and the Crown towns from the Grandees: a paragraph Danvila could not translate. In December, after Tordesillas is retaken, Lope Hurtado de Mendoza describes a badly commanded army and a governor tempted by a deal. One letter read (97.7%), one paragraph read in part (93.5%).

1547

Constantinople · Vienna · France · Truce of Adrianople

Constantinople, 1547: Henri II’s letters to Suleiman, copied by Ferdinand’s spy

Ferdinand I’s resident at the Porte obtains the letters Henri II had the sieur d’Huyson deliver to the Sultan, translates them back from the Turkish and sends them in cipher. To the Sultan, the king asks him to hold the truce void without his Swiss allies, not to leave Hungary to the Habsburgs and to arm his fleet. Three letters read (≈ 97% of groups).

Glückstadt, 1644–1645: Christian Pentz’s cipher letters

The governor of the Elbe fortress writes in cipher to King Christian IV: a stripped garrison, the assault of March 1645, repairs, Spanish money, a raid on Wrangel. A key taken from a period decipherment; one letter read, five read in part.

1715

Pomerania · Saxony · Vienna · Great Northern War

Stralsund, 1715 – Vienna, 1717: Wackerbarth’s ciphered letters

From the camp before Stralsund, the Saxon general tells his wife in Vienna what to answer at the imperial court: a general peace, never a separate one, and the Emperor’s mediation. Two years later he reports Chancellor Sinzendorf’s overture. The 1715 letter read in full, the 1717 report read in part; a simultaneous discovery alongside the work of Anne-Simone Rous.

1858

Funen · Denmark · folk magic

The ciphered grimoire of Kloge Søren

At fifteen, the future healer of Frørup copies out a Cyprianus, a book of charms and recipes, in an alphabet of signs of his own. The key recovered and validated on a held-out portion, the alphabet table in his hand, what the charms say. A partial reading; an earlier decipherment, by Ferdinand Ohrt, is recorded in the archives.

1639

Brussels · Franche-Comté · Switzerland

The cipher table of don Antonio Sarmiento

The son of the ambassador Gondomar, the Cardinal-Infante’s envoy to Franche-Comté and Switzerland, writes in cipher. A twentieth-century copy in Besançon preserves his table: numbers, syllables, words, letter groups. A full transcription, a partial check on a glossed letter, and the lead to the cipher letters in Madrid.

1636

Dole · Antoine Brun · Rossignol

The cipher Rossignol had read

During the siege of Dole, the Parlement and Antoine Brun write in numbers to the relief army. In Paris, Rossignol reads them; a forged letter tries to draw the besieged out; in August they change cipher. The key, rebuilt from the letters received by Girardot de Nozeroy; the text had been in print since 1912.

1932

Tokyo · Japanese Navy · State Department

The Japanese Navy reads the State Department

From January to September 1932, through the Shanghai crisis and the League of Nations inquiry in Manchuria, an office of the Japanese Naval General Staff circulated the clear text of about 850 intercepted American telegrams. Set against the text the State Department published, they show what Tokyo read, and what it did not.

1940

Moscow · Japanese Army · weather reports

Soviet weather read in Tokyo

From August 1938 to October 1940 the Japanese Army’s meteorological service read the Soviet Union’s enciphered weather reports, recovering each new key within hours or days. In 1940 it reconstructed the key tables of the Moscow broadcast: transcribed here, they reproduce exactly the worked example attached to the report.

1825

Madrid · Everett · Zea Bermúdez

What Everett would not write in clear

Spain will never recognise its former colonies, Zea tells the United States minister. In cipher, Everett writes that he does not believe it: a language imposed by the rival party and by Russia. A passage cut from the 1826 printing, and eight pages never printed.

1675

Copenhagen · Griffenfeld · Louis XIV

The price of Danish neutrality

In the spring of 1675 Denmark promises war to the allies at The Hague and secretly bargains over its neutrality with France: 600,000 écus, then 300,000 a year, an engagement handed to Terlon on 11 June and a Swedish marriage to please Louis XIV. Three months later the Scanian War begins.

1663

Afonso VI · Count of Vila Flor

1663 · Lisbon → the Alentejo army

“Even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle.” On 15 May 1663, the day after Don John of Austria invested Évora, Afonso VI ordered the Count of Vila Flor, in cipher, to risk everything to relieve the city. On 26 May, with Évora fallen, the order was repeated. On 8 June came Ameixial. Four ciphered letters, of 13, 15 and 26 May, are read in the record.

1593

Duplessis-Mornay · Tours

1593 · “the king is betrayed”

In 1824 the editors of Duplessis-Mornay's correspondence printed eight cipher passages from two letters of the summer of 1593 as they stood: they had no key. Two centuries later, the “folded” alphabet can be read. At Tours, while the League looks for a king and Henri IV abjures at Saint-Denis, the Protestant leader's correspondents put in cipher what they dare not write in clear: a decree planned to have the Duke of Guise quartered, packets stolen by the Duchess of Angoulême's people, the Count of Gramont in a plot in Béarn, the chancellor and Sourdis behind the truce — “le roy est trahi”, the king is betrayed. Starting hypothesis (“two letters per group”): Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue no. 371).

1675

Copenhagen · Just Høeg

1675 · Copenhagen → The Hague — the Elector wavers

January 1675: the Swedish army has just entered Brandenburg. In Copenhagen, Conrad Biermann, secretary of the German Chancery, copies every week the dispatches leaving for The Hague and Paris; their sensitive passages are in cipher. Thanks to an untitled key sheet in the “Chiffer” volume of the Rigsarkivet, they can be read again: Denmark watches, anxious, as the Elector of Brandenburg wavers — a few months before entering the war against Sweden itself (September 1675, the Scanian War). Thirty-seven letters, January–June 1675, to Høeg and to Meyercrone, read in full: the first published decipherment, to our knowledge.

1710

Charles XII · Bender

1710 · Charles XII, Bender — a “free hand” for an armistice

Bender, 26 April 1710. In exile among the Ottomans, Charles XII — reputed to be closed to any peace — writes in cipher that he is willing to negotiate with Denmark under Anglo-Dutch mediation, and gives the Council a “free hand” for an armistice, “even for a whole year”. Two enciphered copies, forgotten at Stade, read with a reconstructed key.

1532

Ferducci · Fiume

1532 · Ferducci, Fiume — “we shall pretend to go fishing”

Eight enciphered words in a letter otherwise in clear. On 19 July 1532, as Süleyman marched on Vienna, Ferdinand I's agent at Fiume offered to seize the French ambassador at sea on his way back from the sultan — most probably Antonio Rincon. A new reading of an unglossed letter, with a key drawn from contemporary decipherments and confirmed by an independent table of 1542.

1593

Rome · Legate Filippo Sega

Rome’s instruction to the legate, 14 May 1593

Twelve pages of continuous figures: excommunication, a third party, the Infanta’s claim against the Salic law, fear of Navarre’s “feigned conversion”. A probable and partial decipherment; earlier preliminary reading by Satoshi Tomokiyo (2019).

Our method →

01 · The document

Start from the signs

Facsimiles and archive references accompany the transcriptions. A graphical resemblance remains a decision to explain.

02 · The reading

Keep the layers distinct

The image, transcribed sign, proposed value and modernised text are separate. Contextual restorations remain visible.

03 · The evidence

Retain the reservations

A coherent sentence does not prove a key. Unresolved points, corrections and earlier work belong in the dossier.
